claims.text: Kubernetes gives you no such object. What a Veeam Kasten policy protects is defined as a collection of namespaced Kubernetes resources such as ConfigMaps and Secrets, the relevant non-namespaced resources the application uses such as StorageClasses, the Kubernetes workloads themselves — Deployments, StatefulSets, OpenShift DeploymentConfigs and standalone Pods — the deployment and release information available from Helm v3 — Helm is Kubernetes' package manager, covered fully in Module 02, so file the term away rather than chasing it now — and all of the persistent storage resources associated
Not a machine. An application — a set of Kubernetes objects plus its volumes, protected together       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.346]       .
Inside a namespace on a cluster, alongside other applications. Namespace selection is how most policies choose what to protect       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.347]       .
You do not build an inventory by hand. Automatic application discovery is part of the platform       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .
Backing up control-plane components such as etcd and the system namespaces is not the recommended approach here; the focus is the applications       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1092]       .

Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes is a data management platform purpose-built for Kubernetes, providing backup and restore, disaster recovery, and mobility for Kubernetes applications. Its approach is described as application-centric, it is policy-driven, and it exposes a native Kubernetes application programming interface (API) alongside a web-based user interface       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .

Those three capabilities are the product's three principal use cases: backup and restore, disaster recovery, and application mobility       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       . The first two you already own conceptually. The third — mobility — is the one with no clean Veeam Data Platform equivalent, and it is worth knowing why it exists here: because a Kubernetes application is described in portable manifests, an application captured on one cluster can be brought up on another, which makes cross-cluster movement a first-class feature rather than a recovery edge case.
Backup and restore        Protect an application and bring it back — into the same namespace, a different one, or a different cluster       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .
Disaster recovery        Recover when the cluster or the site is gone, including recovering Veeam Kasten's own catalog       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]       .
Application mobility        Move an application and its data across clusters, and potentially across clouds, using a location profile       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315]       .

A policy defines a selection of Kubernetes resources plus one or more data management actions, configured to run on a periodic or event-driven basis. No policies exist after installation; you create every one       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.307]       . Actions can run at hourly, daily, weekly, monthly or yearly granularity, or on demand       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362]       .

For actions that outlive any one cluster, Veeam Kasten needs configured access to external object storage or external NFS or SMB file storage, and that is what a location profile provides. Location profiles are used to create backups from snapshots, to move applications and their data across clusters and potentially across clouds, and to import those backups into another cluster       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315]       .

Resist the habit of treating the target as a folder you can also poke at. The exported data is organised into storage repositories controlled and maintained by the Veeam Kasten instance, and using, connecting to, modifying, copying, or otherwise accessing one of those repositories independently is unsupported and might cause data corruption or loss to some or all of the restore points       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]       . Read-only curiosity is not a safe habit here.

Snapshots are the basis of persistent data capture in Veeam Kasten       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]       . A backup is produced by an     export     , which converts application and volume snapshots into backups by transforming them into an infrastructure-independent format and storing them in a target location       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.351]       .

Application-consistent backups can be enabled where a data service needs quiescing before a volume snapshot: a quiescing function defined in the application                                                                                                           blueprint                                                                       blueprint         A Kanister blueprint is the Kubernetes object that holds the application-specific actions Veeam Kasten calls at defined points in a backup or restore.               is invoked first, then the volume snapshot is taken, and the application i

Application-aware processing is a checkbox. This is an object you deploy and bind. A blueprint is assigned to a workload either by creating a BlueprintBinding or by adding the       kanister.kasten.io/blueprint        annotation, Veeam Kasten looks for blueprints in its own namespace only, and it calls only actions with reserved names such as       backupPrehook        and       backupPosthook        — an action with a name outside that set is silently ignored unless it is configured as a policy action hook       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.890]       . "Silently ignored" is the phrase to underl

Veeam Kasten runs as a set of services inside the cluster, in its own namespace — the install default is       kasten-io              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]        — as Pods you can list. The names show the division of labour:       catalog-svc       ,       executor-svc       ,       crypto-svc       ,       controllermanager-svc       ,       dashboardbff-svc       ,       aggregatedapis-svc       ,       auth-svc       ,       frontend-svc       ,       jobs-svc       ,       kanister-svc        and       state-svc              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.49, p.50]       .

You do not place these. There is no proxy to put on the right subnet and no agent to push to a guest — the platform you are protecting is also the platform that runs the protection, and it decides where those Pods land. Data-moving Pods are created for the work and cleaned up afterwards rather than sitting idle: export Pods are removed by garbage collection after a configured grace period       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1097]       . Your sizing conversation moves from "how many proxies" to "what resources does this cluster have spare".

Backup job                                               Policy       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.307]                                                      Membership is an evaluated selection, not a curated list

Backup repository                                               Location profile       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315]                                                      The target is managed by Veeam Kasten and not yours to touch       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]

Snapshot versus backup                                               Snapshot versus export       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.351]                                                      The export is a separate action you have to enable       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]

Application-aware processing                                               Kanister blueprints and action hooks       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.923]                                                      An object you deploy and bind, with reserved action names       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.890]

Proxies and agents                                               In-cluster services in       kasten-io              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]                                                      You do not size or place them; the cluster does

Three rows of the map, on one screen.          Frequency and retention are the job settings you already know. The toggle in the lower half is the row that matters: snapshots are configured above it, and everything below it exists only because you turned the export on. The Export Location Profile list is where a location profile gets chosen       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]       .

Start with what a snapshot is good at, because it is genuinely good. Snapshots are the basis of persistent data capture in Veeam Kasten, and on most storage systems their performance impact on the primary workload is low, they need no downtime, they restore quickly, and they capture data incrementally       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]       . That is a strong set of properties, and it is why the snapshot action is the one every policy starts from.

Now the limits, stated plainly in the documentation. Storage snapshots suffer from constraints such as relatively low limits on the maximum number of snapshots per volume or per storage array. More importantly, snapshots are not always durable: a catastrophic storage system failure will destroy your snapshots along with your primary data, and on a number of storage systems a snapshot's lifecycle is tied to its source volume, so deleting the volume may garbage-collect every related snapshot at the same time       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]       . The documented guidance that follows is dir

One nuance worth carrying, because it stops this becoming dogma. A number of public cloud providers store snapshots in object storage and retain them independently of the primary volume's lifecycle — though this is not true of all public clouds, and enabling exports in a public cloud may still be worthwhile for safety       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.350]       . "Snapshots are never durable" is too strong; "you do not get to assume they are" is right.

Stage 01 — Snapshot.          Every policy that protects an application starts with the snapshot action, with an optional export action after it to produce a durable backup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.348]. The capture covers the application's Kubernetes resources and a point-in-time copy of its volumes, and it is fast and low-impact [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]. What it is not is independent of the storage system underneath it.

Stage 02 — Export.          To convert snapshots into backups you select     Enable Backups via Snapshot Exports      during policy creation, and the same settings are available when manually exporting a restore point [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]. The export transforms the application and volume snapshots into an infrastructure-independent format and stores them in a target location [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.351]. The backup it produces consists of the application's metadata plus the snapshot data for its volumes, and the metadata destination is an Object Storage Location, an NFS or SMB File

Stage 03 — Restore point.          A restore point is a grouped collection of the data artifacts belonging to an application, and the restore view distinguishes snapshots from backups as well as manual restore points from policy-generated ones. When both a snapshot and a backup exist for the same data, a layered box indicates it, and selecting that layered restore point lets you choose between the local snapshot and the exported backup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.395]. This is the screen that tells you the truth about a policy — if an application only ever shows one kind, you know which action i

A policy with the snapshot action alone will report success indefinitely. Its compliance is fine, its history is green, and its restore points are real — until the storage system that holds them fails, at which point the snapshots go with the primary data       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]       . Nothing in that policy's own status will ever tell you this. The check is structural, not operational: does this policy export, and to where?

The separation is not only a safety mechanism — it is a cost lever, and the documented pattern will look familiar to anyone who has tuned local versus offloaded retention. The guidance is to reduce local retention, which can be more expensive, and increase remote retention, which is more cost-effective; you can run shorter retention on snapshots and extended periods on exports, and you can even split the work across two policies so one snapshots without exporting and the other snapshots and exports       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1092]       .

The two actions are separate all the way down.          Snapshot hooks and export hooks are distinct groups on the same panel, which is the clearest evidence in the interface that these are two stages and not one. This panel is also where a blueprint's hooks get attached to a policy       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.890]       .

Veeam Kasten is deployed into its own namespace,       kasten-io        by convention, and runs as a set of Pods there. After an install you confirm it the same way you would confirm any Kubernetes workload — by listing the Pods in that namespace and waiting for all of them to reach Running       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

That one command replaces a surprising amount of your old troubleshooting surface. There is no proxy server to log into, no agent version to reconcile, and no separate management host: the services listed in the concept map are all Pods in that namespace, and Module 04 covers watching them as the workload they are. Module 03 covers getting them there, which is a Helm install of the       kasten/k10        chart into that namespace       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

The product is Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes, and that is what you call it. You will nonetheless meet the string       k10        constantly and it is not a mistake — it is the chart and release name in the documented install command       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       :

Veeam Kasten is available in two editions       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       . The detail that matters operationally is that both editions use the same container images and follow an identical install process       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.3]        — so the edition question is a licensing conversation, not an architecture one.
It is the default edition and is provided at no charge       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .
Evaluation, or use in small non-production clusters       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .
Functionally it is the same as Enterprise, but limited from a support and scale perspective       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .
Customers choosing to upgrade obtain a license key, or install from cloud marketplaces       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.3]       .
No — the same container images and the same install process as Starter       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.3]       .
The documentation points at the product page for a comparison of the editions rather than listing one       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.3]       .

"Functionally the same" is a phrase to read carefully rather than gratefully. It means a proof of concept on the Starter edition demonstrates real behaviour, which is a genuine advantage. It does not mean a Starter deployment is a supported production deployment — the limits are on support and scale, and both of those are exactly what you need when a restore matters       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.2]       .

A Veeam Repository can serve as the destination for both the application metadata and the persistent volume snapshot data, for any cluster where a Veeam Backup & Replication repository is available and the storage provisioner for the persistent volumes supports block mode export       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.127]       . In location-profile terms it is one more type of target alongside object storage and NFS or SMB file storage       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]       .

What arrives on the other side will look reassuringly familiar. A Veeam Backup & Replication backup job is created on the server for each Veeam Kasten policy, with a Veeam Kasten catalog identifier appended to the job name so that clusters backing up to the same server stay distinct, and each protected application namespace produces a single, separate restore point object. Following export, each backup is converted to a synthetic full backup       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       .

Exporting to a Veeam Repository requires the block mode export mechanism for all volume snapshots the policy creates, and selecting a Veeam Repository as the Export Location Profile enables block mode export automatically       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128]       . The storage provisioner has to be capable of block mode exports       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       .
Export to Veeam Backup & Replication direct object storage repository types is not supported       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128]       .

Each Veeam Kasten instance may export to a single, unique Veeam Backup & Replication backup server. Multiple location profiles may point at separate repositories exposed by that same server, and multiple Veeam Kasten instances may integrate with the same server       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       .

Copies of the backup data produced inside Veeam Backup & Replication — by exporting to a scale-out backup repository (SOBR), by backup copy jobs, or by backup to tape jobs — cannot be directly restored in Veeam Kasten       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       .

All exported volume data is uploaded by a single datamover Pod and stored as a single object in the repository for each export, independent of how many persistent volumes the policy protects       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       .

Read the fourth row again, because it inverts a reflex. Your instinct with any new data source is to get it into the wider protection chain — copy it out, tier it, send it to tape. Those copies remain valid Veeam Backup & Replication restore points and you may well still want them, but Veeam Kasten cannot restore an application directly from them       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       . Decide deliberately which copy is the one your Kubernetes recovery plan depends on, and write it down.

Two more things worth holding from this section. A manual export that is not associated with a policy produces a standalone       K10ManualBackup        backup job containing the application namespace, saved as a full, independent VeeamZIP backup       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]       . And an exported restore point can be imported and restored on another supported cluster, provided the target cluster is configured with the same Veeam Repository location profile used for the volume data       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129]        — which is application mobility using storage you already ru

The application is the unit of protection.                    Veeam Kasten works at that level: it discovers applications on the cluster it runs in and protects them as whole objects                                                                                                            — stateful and stateless parts together                                                                        Application object         Veeam Kasten's application object encapsulates information about all stateful and stateless resources that make up the application       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]

The control plane is not your backup target either.                    Veeam Kasten is built to protect Kubernetes applications and cannot be used to deploy or restore a cluster's overall state, so cluster build-out stays with your infrastructure-as-code tooling       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

The word "cluster" means something different on each side of this comparison. A vSphere cluster is a grouping of hosts inside a larger inventory. A Kubernetes cluster is the entire management domain — its own API, its own accounts, its own set of nodes. Two Kubernetes clusters are two separate worlds, which is exactly why moving an application between clusters is treated as a restore operation rather than a migration wizard       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Rebuild a stateless front end from its declaration and you have lost nothing. Rebuild a database from its declaration and you have an empty database. That asymmetry is the entire reason a Kubernetes backup product exists, and it is visible in how Veeam Kasten presents a cluster: its dashboard can filter down to only the applications that have stateful services, which it defines as applications containing a persistent volume       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       .

Veeam Kasten classifies Pods, VirtualMachines, StatefulSets, Deployments, and DeploymentConfigs as     workloads     , and treats an application as something made up of multiple Kubernetes resources and workloads together       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.303]       . So a single application card in its dashboard may account for several volumes, several network resources, several workloads, and additional configuration objects at once       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.303]       .

Do not read "StatefulSet" as "everything with data". Some modern data services are managed by their own custom controllers rather than by a StatefulSet, and Veeam Kasten added support for pre- and post-snapshot Blueprint actions for those custom-resource-managed workloads by mapping Pod and volume-claim ownership when a policy runs       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096]       . The reliable signal that data is present is a persistent volume, not the controller type.

A crash-consistent volume snapshot is not always enough for a database, exactly as it is not in a virtual estate. Veeam Kasten handles that case with Kanister Blueprints, which run pre- and post-backup hooks for workloads that need application-specific work such as pausing a database before a backup or migration       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       . You will meet these again when you build policies.

A         namespace          is a named boundary inside a cluster that holds a set of related objects — workloads, configuration, secrets, storage claims, service definitions. Names are unique within a namespace rather than across the cluster, access control is commonly granted per namespace, and a team is commonly given one to work in. (On Red Hat OpenShift, which this course also targets, the same boundary surfaces as a         Project          — Veeam Kasten's own OpenShift install instructions treat the two words as one thing, telling you to create "a project (namespace)" for the installat

That convention is load-bearing for Veeam Kasten. The platform by default equates namespaces to applications — for ease of use, for consistency with Kubernetes practice and role-based access control, and because it mirrors the most common application deployment pattern       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       . It is a default, not a cage: policies can be defined to operate on more than one namespace, or on only a subset of an application that lives inside a single namespace       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       .

Some of the application is not in the namespace at all.                    Cluster-scoped objects such as StorageClasses and custom resource definitions live outside every namespace, and an application that depends on them needs a policy that protects both the application and its cluster-scoped resources       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.429]       .

Applications, counted for you.          Nobody registered these applications by hand. Veeam Kasten abstracts each application it has automatically discovered on the cluster it is running in       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]       , then reports each one as unmanaged when no protection policy covers it, non-compliant when a policy applies but its actions are failing or have not run yet, and compliant when a policy applies and its service-level agreements (SLAs) are being respected       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       .

Discovery is the part of onboarding a new estate that costs the most in a virtual environment: finding everything, deciding what is in scope, keeping the list current as people build things. Here the inventory maintains itself, and the interesting number on that dashboard is the unmanaged count — the applications that exist and are not yet covered by any policy       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       . That number is your work queue.

Stage 02 — the class.          A StorageClass is the cluster's catalogue entry: a name a claim can ask for, plus the provisioner and parameters behind it. Closest instinct: a storage policy in a virtual estate. Where it breaks: a StorageClass is cluster-scoped, so it is not inside the namespace it serves — which is why protecting an application sometimes means protecting cluster-scoped resources alongside it       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.429]       .

Stage 03 — the driver.          The provisioner named by the class does the work against the storage system. Where a platform offers both a CSI driver and an older in-tree provisioner, the CSI provisioner is the one to choose: the legacy in-tree provisioners are deprecated and will be removed in later Kubernetes versions, and claims made by them are being migrated to CSI drivers       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

In a virtual estate the storage layer is largely an implementation detail of the backup design: the hypervisor presents disks, and your backup server reads them. Here the storage layer is a first-class dependency, because the ability to take a fast, consistent point-in-time copy belongs to the driver rather than to the backup product. Veeam Kasten supports direct integration with a set of storage providers — among them Amazon Elastic Block Store, Azure Managed Disks, Google Persistent Disk, Ceph, Cinder-based providers on OpenStack, vSphere Cloud Native Storage, Portworx, and Veeam Backup — as

Two practical consequences follow. First, a storage system with no CSI driver that can snapshot pushes you onto a file-copy-based path: Veeam Kasten supports Generic Storage Backups for such systems, and the documentation states plainly that this approach is not recommended       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       . Most NFS storage services on the market do not provide a CSI driver with snapshot and clone capabilities, and migrating persistent data to storage that does is the recommended course       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       . Second, snapshot limits are a design input: verify

Veeam Kasten can invoke volume snapshot operations through CSI, and three requirements have to be met for that to work: Kubernetes v1.14.0 or higher, the       VolumeSnapshotDataSource        feature enabled in the cluster, and a CSI driver that has Volume Snapshot support       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . Using a CSI driver with VolumeSnapshot support is described as a requirement for building a good data protection solution with Veeam Kasten       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Whether a CSI provisioner supports VolumeSnapshots may be stated in the storage vendor's documentation, and it can also be validated with Veeam Kasten's own tooling rather than taken on trust       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Run with a specified StorageClass, the primer tool — the pre-flight tool you install and run in Module 03 — runs in a Pod in the cluster and creates a sample application with a persistent volume, writes data to it, snapshots the volume, creates a new volume from that snapshot, and validates the data in the new volume       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . Module 03 covers both invocations: the basic run, and this one.

For each CSI driver, a VolumeSnapshotClass has to carry the Veeam Kasten annotation before its snapshots can be used       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . You will apply it in Module 03; recognise it here.

The annotation and class name above are quoted from the Storage Integration reference       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       .       k10        appears in lowercase inside the annotation key       k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class        because that key is a verbatim technical string; the product name is Veeam Kasten.

CSI snapshots are not durable. A snapshot has a namespaced VolumeSnapshot object and a non-namespaced VolumeSnapshotContent object, and with the default and recommended deletion policy, deleting the volume or the namespace containing it cleans up the namespaced object and cascades into deleting the VolumeSnapshotContent object and therefore the underlying storage snapshot       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . Setting       deletionPolicy        to       Delete        is not sufficient either, because some storage systems force snapshot deletion when the associated volume is deleted, and

One namespace deletion can take the snapshots with it.                    In a virtual estate, deleting a VM does not commonly reach into the array and remove its snapshots. Here the cascade is documented behaviour       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       .

Veeam Kasten defends the copy it restores from.                    It creates a clone of the original VolumeSnapshotClass with the deletion policy set to       Retain       , and when restoring a CSI VolumeSnapshot it creates an independent replica using that cloned class to avoid accidental deletion of the underlying content       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       .

Chart repository         A location Helm pulls charts from. Veeam Kasten's charts come from the Kasten Helm charts repository, which you add to Helm before installing       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

Chart version and product version         The chart version selects which Veeam Kasten version you install, so pinning it is how you control what lands in the cluster       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.759]       .
Release name         The name you give the installation. Veeam Kasten's documented install names the release       k10              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .
Target namespace         Where the release's objects are created. The Veeam Kasten install default is       kasten-io              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

Read it as three sentences: know where the charts live, refresh that knowledge, then create a release called       k10        from the       kasten/k10        chart inside the       kasten-io        namespace. Commands quoted from the install reference       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

Helm is not the only route in. On Red Hat OpenShift there are two documented methods to install Veeam Kasten — a Helm-based installation and an Operator-based installation       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.53]       . Whichever you choose, the documentation encourages automating that deployment as part of the same tooling that builds the cluster, so that after a total cluster loss you can rebuild the platform and then recover applications and data with Veeam Kasten       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Two version checks save time later. The Helm 3 package manager has to be in place before installing, and its version should be compatible with the version of the Kubernetes cluster you are deploying into       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       . Veeam Kasten's Helm chart can also be signature-verified with the published public key during installation       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

Veeam Kasten does not sit beside the cluster looking in. It runs     inside      the cluster, as a set of its own services in their own namespace. The install default for that namespace is       kasten-io              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       , and after installing, the way you confirm the platform is healthy is to watch its Pods reach a running state       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

Those services are individually named — an aggregated API service, an authentication service, a catalog service and others appear in the Pod list       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]        — and Veeam Kasten's own tooling talks about validating a cluster before installation and debugging the platform's micro services afterwards       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.866]       . Read that as a design statement: this is not one monolithic server process, it is a set of cooperating in-cluster components.

The documented validation step. All of the Pods should ultimately display a status of       Running       ; it may take a couple of minutes for them to come up       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

It discovers instead of being told        Veeam Kasten's application object abstracts an application that has been automatically discovered on the cluster where Veeam Kasten is running, and captures its stateful and stateless resources together       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]       . There is no inventory to register and no agent to push.

It speaks the cluster's own language        Policies encode business rules and translate them into the actions Veeam Kasten applies to the applications it has discovered       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]       . Its own objects — policies, profiles, actions, restore points — live in the cluster API like any other Kubernetes resource.

It is hardened as an in-cluster tenant        Because it runs as Pods among other Pods, its security posture is a cluster concern: all Veeam Kasten Pods enable a read-only root filesystem security context by default, with writable paths backed by dedicated volume mounts       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096]       . Apart from direct storage provider integration, Veeam Kasten also supports invoking volume snapshot operations via the Container Storage Interface [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. This is the path most on-premises clusters take, and it needs one specific thing from you.

If an existing VolumeSnapshotClass does not match the required configuration, the documentation shows how to modify it, and if it cannot be modified, a new one can be created with the required annotation [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103]. Whenever Veeam Kasten detects volumes that were provisioned via a CSI driver, it will look for a VolumeSnapshotClass with the Veeam Kasten annotation for the identified CSI driver and use it to create snapshots [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103]. An existing VolumeSnapshotClass can be annotated in place [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].

Verify that only one VolumeSnapshotClass per storage provisioner has the Veeam Kasten annotation — currently, if no VolumeSnapshotClass or more than one has the Veeam Kasten annotation, snapshot operations will fail [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103]. Two annotated classes is the failure mode that looks like nothing at install time and shows up later as failed snapshots.
The check is one command. List the VolumeSnapshotClasses that carry the annotation and count the answers per provisioner [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].

As an alternative to annotating the VolumeSnapshotClass, a StorageClass can be annotated instead, and all volumes created with that StorageClass will be snapshotted by the specified VolumeSnapshotClass [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].

Cross-cluster names must match.          If application migration across clusters is needed, ensure that the VolumeSnapshotClass names match between both clusters; as the VolumeSnapshotClass is also used for restoring volumes, an identical name is required [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].

The snapshotter has a floor.          Ensure that the csi-snapshotter container for all CSI drivers you might have installed has a minimum version of v1.2.2 [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103] — the documentation states this as a hard minimum, so treat it as a check to make before your first policy runs, not a diagnosis to reach for after one fails.
CSI snapshots are not durable [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].

With the default and recommended deletionPolicy, deleting a volume or the namespace containing it leads to a cascading delete of the VolumeSnapshotContent object and therefore the underlying storage snapshot [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
Setting deletionPolicy to Delete isn't sufficient either, as some storage systems will force snapshot deletion if the associated volume is deleted [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
Enabling backups together with volume snapshots is therefore required for a durable backup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].

Veeam Kasten protects the restore path.                    Veeam Kasten creates a clone of the original VolumeSnapshotClass with the DeletionPolicy set to 'Retain', so that when restoring a CSI VolumeSnapshot an independent replica is created using this cloned class to avoid accidental deletions of the underlying VolumeSnapshotContent [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].

The top of the Veeam Kasten dashboard shows the applications on the cluster, the policies that exist, and a summary of the cluster's backup data footprint [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]. Filtered to applications with stateful services, each is placed in one of four states — the closest thing here to your morning read of job sessions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Unmanaged        No protection policy covers this object [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].
Non-compliant        A policy applies, but its actions are failing or have not been invoked yet — for example, right after policy creation [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301].

Veeam Kasten enables centralized monitoring of its activity by integrating with Prometheus, exposing a Prometheus endpoint that a central system can extract data from [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.746]. Leave that server enabled. Disabling it reduces functionality in various parts of the system, including usage data, reporting, and the multi-cluster dashboard; if it has been disabled, it can be re-enabled during a Helm upgrade with       --set prometheus.server.enabled=true        [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.763].

Action metrics are the ones you will query first. Veeam Kasten records counts for cluster and application-specific actions, labels them with the action's context, and includes the final status as       state        for ended actions — with an action's state reported as values including       pending       ,       running       ,       attempt_failed       ,       failed       ,       succeeded       ,       cancelled       ,       skipped       , and       deleting        [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.748].

Veeam Kasten is a stateful application running on the cluster, so it must be responsible for backing up its own data to enable recovery in the event of disaster — the backup enabled by the Veeam Kasten Disaster Recovery (KDR) policy [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565]. KDR provides the ability to recover the Veeam Kasten platform from a variety of disasters: unintended deletion of Veeam Kasten or its restore points, failure of the underlying storage used by Veeam Kasten, or accidental destruction of the Kubernetes cluster Veeam Kasten is deployed on [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565]. And check your intended target: Veeam Repository location profiles cannot be used as a destination for KDR backups [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.572]. Stage 01 — export off-site.          The documented rebuild strategy starts by configuring policies to export backups to an off-site location [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Without this, KDR recovers a catalog that points at data the surviving site cannot read.

Stage 03 — new cluster.          In the event of a complete cluster or site loss, a new cluster can be deployed in a secondary site or the public cloud [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. In the dashboard this is the Restore Kasten page, which asks for the location profile holding the exported KDR backups, the cluster identifier of the source instance, and the passphrase method used at setup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.572].

Stage 05 in the dashboard.          Recovering an instance asks for the location profile, the cluster identifier of the source instance, and the passphrase used when the KDR policy was configured — then a restore point and a summary [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571, p.572]. Every field on this screen is something you decided months earlier, which is why the passphrase belongs in your secrets store and your runbook, not in someone's memory.

Veeam Kasten catalog backup and restore are handled through this dedicated disaster recovery process, and the guide's recommendation is to enable Veeam Kasten DR and regularly test the process [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Treat the KDR test like the restore tests you already run: on a schedule, with the passphrase retrieved from where it is meant to live rather than from your own notes.

"Who backs up the backup system?" is the question that ends a lot of Kubernetes protection projects late. The answer here is concrete and demonstrable: the platform runs a dedicated policy over its own namespace, exports the catalog to an external location profile you choose — one that supports immutable backups, so the catalog survives ransomware and accidental deletion — and encrypts it with a passphrase held in a passphrase provider, then recovers onto a new cluster from that export [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.565, p.571, p.1093].

Veeam Kasten provides a way to collect and clean up resources that are either orphaned or whose expiration period has passed, through a garbage collector daemon [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.839]. Three Helm options tune it:       garbagecollector.daemonPeriod        sets the length of time between two consecutive garbage collection events in seconds,       garbagecollector.keepMaxActions        sets how many finished actions to keep — with no actions deleted if the value is less than or equal to zero — and       garbagecollector.actions.enabled        enables the action collectors [Src: Kasten Do

What the daemon cleans is a specific list: actions above the retained maximum, oldest first and handled independently per action type;       RestorePointContents        for expired manual backups, as determined by their       expiresAt        value; and the temporary objects left behind by restore operations —       CSISnapshot        objects, persistent volumes, profiles, services, network policies, secrets, and config maps [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.839]. Export pods are cleaned up by the garbage collection daemon after the configured grace period [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1097].

When restore points are retired — manually or through a policy retention schedule — Veeam Kasten cleans up the associated resources, but the cleanup is not immediate for all of them; backup data in an object store may take a significant amount of time to be removed [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.365]. Protecting an application with Veeam Kasten, which is accomplished by creating a policy, rests on three concepts:         snapshots and exports          (one or both of the data-capture mechanisms),         scheduling          (capture frequency plus snapshot and backup retention objectives), and         selection          (which applications the policy protects, with resource filtering when finer control is needed) [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.346]. If you read "job settings, schedule, and job scope" while you read that sentence, your mental model is close enough to start.

What a policy protects is an     application     , and Veeam Kasten defines that term precisely: a collection of namespaced Kubernetes resources, the relevant non-namespaced resources the application uses, the Kubernetes workloads, deployment and release information available from Helm v3, and all of the persistent storage resources associated with those workloads [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.346]. A new policy can be created from the Policies page or from the Applications page, and starting from the Applications page pre-populates the policy name and the namespace selection [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0

All policies center on the execution of actions, and for protecting applications you start with the snapshot action and add an optional export action to produce a durable backup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.348]. Those are not two names for one thing. The difference is the single most important idea in this module, because it decides where a restore can come from.
Where does it live?                              On the storage system that holds the volumes, alongside the primary data [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349].
What is it good at?                              Low performance impact on the primary workload, no downtime, fast restore times, and incremental data capture [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349].

Where does it fall down?                              Storage systems set relatively low limits on snapshots per volume or per array, and snapshots are not always durable: catastrophic storage failure destroys them along with the primary data, and in a number of systems a snapshot's lifecycle is tied to the source volume, so deleting the volume can garbage-collect the snapshots with it [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349].

Where does it live?                              In a target location outside the cluster's primary storage. The metadata destination is an Object Storage Location, an NFS/SMB File Storage Location, or a Veeam Repository Location, named in the Export Location Profile field [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352].

What is it good at?                              Export operations convert application and volume snapshots into backups by transforming them into an infrastructure-independent format and storing them in that target location [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.351] — which is what makes them durable, portable, and restorable on a different cluster.

How do I turn it on?                              Select         Enable Backups via Snapshot Exports          during policy creation; the destination and the control over exporting snapshot data versus a reference appear there too [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352].

A snapshot-only policy is a policy with no durable copy. Because of the limitations of snapshots, setting up backups of your application stack is advisable, and durable backups are created by exporting data [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]. Treat "snapshot plus export" as the default shape of a production policy and make yourself justify any policy that stops at the snapshot.

Exported data is organized into storage repositories that are exclusively controlled and maintained by the Veeam Kasten instance. Independently using, interacting with, connecting to, modifying, copying, upgrading, or in any way accessing or manipulating a Veeam Kasten storage repository is unsupported and can cause data corruption or loss to some or all of the restore points [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.352]. Whatever housekeeping habits you have for a backup repository you can browse, leave them at the door for this one.

Scheduling in Veeam Kasten breaks into four components: how frequently the primary snapshot action runs, how often snapshots are exported into backups, the retention schedule of snapshots and backups, and when the primary snapshot action runs [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362]. Work through them in that order and the form stops feeling crowded.

Actions can be set to execute at an hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly granularity, or on demand. By default, actions set to hourly execute at the top of the hour and other actions execute at midnight UTC [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362]. You can also select the time at which scheduled actions execute, and sub-frequencies that run multiple actions per frequency [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362].

Sub-hourly actions are useful when what you are protecting is chiefly Kubernetes objects or small data sets; care should be taken with more general-purpose workloads because of the risk of stressing the underlying storage infrastructure or running into storage API rate limits [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362]. Sub-frequencies also interact with retention: retaining 24 hourly snapshots at 15-minute intervals would only retain six hours of snapshots [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362]. That single sentence has caught out more people than any other line on this page.

Backups performed via exports are, by default, set up to export every snapshot into a backup, and it is also possible to select a subset of snapshots for exports — for example, converting only every daily snapshot into a backup [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.362]. That subset choice is the lever you pull when hourly snapshots are cheap on the array and expensive in the object store.

One constraint to design around before you save: to maintain backup recovery points, once the policy is saved the export location profile can only be changed to a compatible location profile. The interface enforces compatibility when you edit a policy, but no compatibility enforcement is performed when editing the policy custom resource directly [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.363].

Veeam Kasten can use a grandfather-father-son (GFS) retention scheme for cost and compliance reasons. Under that backup rotation scheme, hourly snapshots and backups rotate on an hourly basis with one graduating to daily every day, and so on; you set the number of hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly copies to retain, and Veeam Kasten handles both cleanup at every retention tier and graduation to the next one. For on-demand policies it is not possible to set a retention schedule [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.364].

Backup retention schedules default to the same values as snapshot retention schedules, and can be set to independent schedules if needed — which lets you keep a limited number of snapshots for fast recovery from accidental outages while storing a larger number of backups for long-term recovery needs [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.364].

Two behaviors worth knowing before they surprise you. The retention schedule for a policy does not apply to snapshots and backups produced by manual policy runs; any artifacts created by a manual run need to be cleaned up manually [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.364]. And restore points created by failed policy runs do not count towards retiring older restore points — they are retained until there are enough newer restore points from successful runs to satisfy the retention counts, which can leave you with more restore points than you expected while a policy is failing [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.364]

The Advanced Options settings let you pick how many times and when actions execute within the interval of the frequency — for a daily frequency, which hour or hours within each day and which minute within each hour [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.366]. By default hourly retention counts apply to the hourly action at the top of the hour, daily counts to the action at midnight, weekly counts to midnight Sunday, monthly counts to midnight on the first of each month, and yearly counts to midnight on 1 January, all in UTC [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.366]. If the policy has an hourly frequency and the window exceeds one hour, the policy is also scheduled to run every 60 minutes thereafter within the window [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.367].

With staggering enabled, Veeam Kasten automatically finds an optimal start time and runs the policy within the selected interval, which lets it stagger runs of multiple policies and reduce peak load on the overall system [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.367].

Set expectations on duration before you promise anything to an application owner. A restore can take a few minutes, depending on the amount of data captured by the restore point, and the time is dominated by how long it takes to rehydrate captured data followed by recreating the application containers, so it tracks the speed of the underlying storage infrastructure [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.392]. The word "export" in the interface does not mean you need an import policy to use the result. While the interface uses the Export term for backups, no import policy is needed to restore from a backup; import policies are only needed when you want to restore the application into a different cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.395]. Restoring on the same cluster from an exported backup is the ordinary restore workflow.

The local snapshot is the fast path while the storage under it is intact — snapshots support fast restore times and implement incremental data capture, with low performance impact on the primary workload [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]. The exported backup would also work, and would cost you a rehydration you did not need to pay for.

This is the scenario the export tier exists for. Snapshots are not always durable: catastrophic storage system failure destroys your snapshots along with your primary data, and in a number of storage systems a snapshot's lifecycle is tied to the source volume [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.349]. The exported backup sits in an infrastructure-independent format in a separate target location [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.351], which is why it survives.

By default Veeam Kasten restores applications into the original namespace the restore point was created from, but the target namespace can be changed and new namespaces can be created at that point; debugging, test and development, and cloning are documented uses of exactly that [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.416]. Restoring in place would recreate the entire application stack into the selected namespace [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.396] — an outage you did not need to take.

Veeam Kasten provides the       FileRecoverySession        custom resource to request network access to files from exported restore points without requiring a full restore of volume data [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.419]. A Volume-Clones restore is the next-best answer and a good one: it restores individual volumes into the existing application namespace without disrupting its operation or workloads [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.408], though you then mount and copy by hand. A full application restore is the sledgehammer.
You need the applications running on a cluster that has never seen them.

Import policies are supported for importing applications into a cluster that is different from where the application was captured [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.460], and this is the path Section 03 walks. Is the local snapshot still trustworthy? If the storage under it is intact, take the snapshot; if the storage failed, take the exported backup, because that is the copy in an infrastructure-independent format outside the cluster's primary storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.351]. Then: does the data have to land on top of the running application? If not, restore into a different namespace instead, which is a supported target choice at restore time [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.416]. At overview depth: how an export policy on one cluster and an import policy on another combine into a path that lands a running application somewhere it has never run. By the end of this section you can name the four stages, say which policy setting decides whether the path works at all, and explain what an import policy does when nobody has asked for a restore yet.

The workflow for exporting applications into another cluster is close to the workflow for protecting them: when a policy is created to capture an application, you also select the Enable Backups via Snapshot Exports option, and one export action is created for each backup action when the export schedule triggers. Once all the export actions finish for that scheduled time, the metadata is uploaded to the location specified by the profile, and after that upload the backups are available for import [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.455].

That "available for import" is the hinge. Nothing about the export knows which cluster will consume it. Location profiles are also used for importing applications into a cluster that is different from the source cluster where the application was captured [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.338] — the shared location is the whole handshake, plus one encoded string.

This is the setting that decides whether the path works: if migration is desired across Kubernetes clusters in different clouds or between on-premises and public cloud environments, the Export Snapshot Data option must be enabled to migrate both the application data and the metadata, because without it the application data

For a manual export, the encoded import configuration required by the destination cluster is presented after you confirm the export [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.459]. Treat that string the way you treat any other credential material — it is what allows the destination cluster to establish the data export and

You also specify a frequency, but that frequency only controls how often to check the shared object storage or file storage location; if data in the store is not refreshed at the same frequency no duplicate work is performed, and multiple restore points may be imported by a single action if there is catching-up to do [Src: Kas

Stage 04 — Restore, then or later.          After the Create Policy button is clicked the system starts scheduling jobs based on the policy definition; when new data is detected its metadata is imported into the cluster, associated with the application stack already running, and made available as a restore point [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.464]. Unless         Restore after Import          is selected, only metadata is brought into the cluster, and data volumes residing in an object store or file store are not converted into native volumes until a restore operation is initiated [Src: Kasten Docs

Care should be taken when auto-restoring the application during import: ensure the newly restored application does not conflict with the application running in the source cluster, and examples of potential conflicts include accidental credential reuse, access to and use of external services, and services conflicting for exclusive ownership of shared resources [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.462]. Two live copies of the same application, both convinced they own the same external queue, is a failure mode you cause rather than suffer.

Running an import policy keeps the list of local restore points in sync with the retention settings of the originating policy. If a restore point is marked for retirement by the source cluster it is cleaned up, and the next time the import policy runs that retired restore point is removed from the destination cluster, reflecting the fact that it can no longer be used to restore the application [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.464].

By default Veeam Kasten restores Kubernetes resources as they exist in the restore point, but when the restore target does not match the environment of the backup, resource artifacts can be transformed on restore — for example, updating container image URLs or changing storage class settings when moving between cloud providers [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.464]. Transforms are applied by enabling         Apply transforms to restored resources          under Restore After Import [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.465].

Import is for crossing cluster boundaries. The entire application stack can be migrated across different namespaces in the same cluster, and that is covered by the restore workflow rather than by an import policy [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.451]. If you find yourself building an import policy to move a namespace inside one cluster, stop and go back to Section 02.

Service accounts are bound through the same form, using a naming convention rather than a separate control. Bindings are available for the subject types Users and Groups; where a service account binding is required, the format       system:serviceaccount:<sa_namespace>:<sa_name>        is used in the User field for a single service account in a specific namespace, or the format       system:serviceaccounts:<sa_name>        is used in the Group field for a service account in all namespaces [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.280].

Granting people the ability to manage access is a bigger grant than it looks. Viewing and managing Veeam Kasten-specific Kubernetes RBAC resources from the dashboard requires additional permissions, and while a read-only view can be granted with list and get verbs, additional verbs such as create, update, and delete should be added with caution because they allow those users to escalate their own privileges [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.277][Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.278].

Its filtering is what makes it a weekly tool rather than a lookup. Filtering by type lets you identify local snapshot-based restore points, exported restore points managed by the cluster, or imported restore points created by another cluster; selecting         Include manual runs only          lists the restore points created by backup or export actions that are not associated with a policy, or by manually

Pair those two filters together — manual runs only, no expiration — and run it weekly. Artifacts from manual runs are outside the policy's retention schedule and must be cleaned up manually [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.364], and that pair of filters is how you find the ones you forgot. The strongest operational guidance in the documentation is also the easiest to postpone: test restores regularly and do not wait for a disaster to happen, testing application restores within the same namespace, in a different namespace on the same Kubernetes cluster, and on different clusters [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Test granular application restores as well as full application restores, and restore applications based on priority to meet recovery time objective (RTO) requirements [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Those three destinations map exactly onto the three paths in Section 02,

To optimize storage costs, the documented recommendation is to reduce local retention, which can be more expensive, and increase remote retention, and to strike a balance that prevents storage from filling up [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1092]. Shorter on snapshots and extended periods for exports is the same advice from the policy side [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

Avoid creating a policy with a wildcard namespace selector; create policies per application or per application group and use the backup window and staggering instead, which reduces load on both Veeam Kasten and the cluster API [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Define a backup window that does not conflict with multiple policies, to prevent system overload [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

Use a policy preset to standardize backup and export retention across policies, configure a dedicated policy for protecting cluster-scoped resources, and use labels to target specific resources so one policy can serve a group of them [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Presets are what make self-service safe: each policy created from a preset refers to it rather than copying it, so every preset change also changes the corresponding policies [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.384].

Regularly verify the readiness of your applications; if they are scaled down, experiencing issues, or not functioning correctly, enabling the "Ignore Exceptions and Continue if Possible" option in the policy actions ensures they are carried out to the best of their ability [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

Veeam Kasten provides metrics about its activities; the documented approach is to gather them with Prometheus to track backups, restores, and overall system health, visualize them in Grafana, and configure alerts when metrics exceed critical levels [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. Creating alerts for any actions where       state=failed        is recommended, along with an alert for catalog volume used space above 50 percent, because that condition can affect upgrades [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].

Regularly check the metrics and logs of your Veeam Kasten system, which helps you find and fix problems before they lead to downtime or data loss, and keep the monitoring configuration up to date as the deployment evolves so you monitor the right metrics and receive alerts for new issues [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].
